blocks.text: If you have read through the earlier lessons on tools, resources, prompts, and transports, you already understand the shape of MCP conceptually, messages flowing back and forth in a well defined protocol.
The Python SDK is where that theory turns into code you can actually run.

It is the official library maintained alongside the MCP specification itself, and its whole purpose is to let you write a working server or client without hand rolling JSON-RPC message parsing, capability negotiation, or transport plumbing.
You write ordinary Python functions, decorate them, and the SDK handles the rest.
1. What the SDK Is and Why It Exists

blocks.alt: Python code decorated with SDK helpers becomes a full MCP server

blocks.text: Underneath every MCP server sits the same obligations: advertise capabilities during initialization, respond to tools/list and tools/call, serialize results correctly, keep track of request IDs, and speak whichever transport the host expects.

None of that is intellectually hard, but it is exactly the kind of boilerplate that, if every server author wrote it by hand, would produce a hundred slightly different and subtly buggy implementations.
The Python SDK exists to write that plumbing once, correctly, so that the only thing left for you to write is your actual logic.

Think of it the way you might think of a web framework. You could write raw socket handling and HTTP parsing yourself, but almost nobody does, because a framework already solved that problem well. The Python SDK plays the same role for MCP, letting you focus on what your server actually does, reading files, querying a database, calling an external API, rather than on how JSON-RPC envelopes are assembled.
2. Installing and Setting Up a Project

A typical project starts with a normal Python virtual environment and a single package install. From there, a server is usually just one file to begin with, growing into a small package as it takes on more tools and resources.

code.content:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install mcp

# project layout for a small server
my-server/
  .venv/
  server.py
  pyproject.toml

blocks.text: Nothing here is exotic. If you have set up any other Python package before, this will feel completely familiar. The SDK itself has very few hard dependencies, which keeps a freshly generated server lightweight and quick to install.
3. The Server Object and Entry Point

Every server built with the SDK starts by constructing a server instance and giving it a name. That instance is the object every decorator attaches to, and it is also what eventually gets handed to a transport function that starts listening for messages.

code.content:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("notes-server")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()

blocks.text: This tiny snippet is already a complete, if empty, MCP server. It will start up, complete initialization with any host that connects to it, and correctly report that it has no tools, resources, or prompts yet. Everything from here is additive, you register capabilities one decorator at a time.
4. Registering Tools with a Decorator

blocks.alt: A decorator turns a plain function into a registered tool

blocks.text: Turning an ordinary function into an MCP tool is usually a single line, a decorator placed directly above the function definition. The function's name becomes the tool's name by default, its docstring becomes the tool's description, and its parameters become the tool's input schema.

Notice how little of this is MCP specific. Aside from the decorator, this reads like a plain utility function you might already have lying around, and that is deliberate, the SDK is designed so that exposing existing logic as a tool costs almost nothing extra.

You can also override the default name and description explicitly, which is useful when a function's Python name is not the friendliest thing to show a model, or when the docstring needs to stay short for readability but the tool description should say more.
5. Type Hints and Automatic Schema Generation

blocks.alt: Type hints on a function generate the input schema automatically

blocks.text: The SDK reads a decorated function's type hints and builds a JSON Schema for its input automatically, so a client calling tools/list sees a proper schema without you writing one by hand. A str becomes a string schema, an int becomes an integer schema, an Optional or default value marks a parameter as not required.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Python type hint","Resulting schema type"],"rows":[["str","string"],["int","integer"],["float","number"],["bool","boolean"],["list[str]","array of string"],["a Pydantic model","a nested object schema"]]}

blocks.text: For anything more structured than a handful of primitive parameters, defining a small Pydantic model as the function's single argument keeps the tool signature clean while still producing a rich, well validated schema on the wire.
6. Registering Resources

Resources use a similar decorator, but instead of a plain function name, they are tied to a URI or a URI template. The function returns the resource's content directly, and the SDK takes care of wrapping it into a proper resources/read response.

A resource function is usually read only and side effect free, since its whole job is to answer "what does this look like right now," not to change anything. Keeping that boundary clean makes a server's behavior far easier to reason about.
7. Resource Templates with URI Parameters

When a resource represents one of many similar items, a note by its ID, a file by its path, the SDK supports templated URIs where curly brace segments become function parameters automatically, extracted straight out of the requested URI string.

A client discovers this pattern through resources/templates/list, sees the placeholder, and can construct a concrete URI like notes://a1b2c3 to fetch one specific note, without the server needing to enumerate every possible note ID up front.
8. Registering Prompts

Prompts are reusable message templates a host can surface to a user, and the SDK registers them the same decorator driven way, with parameters again derived from the function signature. A prompt function typically returns either a string or a small list of structured messages.

Because a prompt is just text or structured messages returned from a function, it can pull in live data the same way a tool or resource can, interpolating today's note content into the template rather than hardcoding a static string.
9. Handling Structured Input and Output

For tools with more than a couple of parameters, or ones that return more than a plain string or number, Pydantic models pull double duty as both the schema source and the runtime validator. If a client sends malformed input, the SDK raises a validation error before your function body even runs.
10. Async Support and Long-Running Tools

blocks.alt: A long running tool uses async support to avoid blocking the server

blocks.text: Any tool, resource, or prompt function can be declared async def instead of a plain def, and the SDK will await it correctly. This matters enormously for tools that call out to a network service, a database, or another slow operation, since a synchronous function would otherwise block the whole server from handling anything else in the meantime.

code.content:
@mcp.tool()
async def fetch_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Fetch the current weather for a city from an external API."""
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        resp = await client.get(f"https://api.example.com/weather/{city}")
        data = resp.json()
        return f"{data['temp_c']} C, {data['condition']}"

blocks.text: There is no special flag needed to opt into async, the SDK simply inspects whether the function you registered is a coroutine and awaits it if so, otherwise it runs it directly.
11. The Context Object: Logging, Progress, and Sampling

blocks.alt: The context object provides logging, progress, and sampling to a tool

blocks.text: A tool function can optionally accept a context parameter, giving it access to capabilities beyond its own inputs and outputs, sending log messages back to the client, reporting incremental progress on a long operation, or even asking the host to run a sampling request against a language model on the tool's behalf.

code.content:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import Context

@mcp.tool()
async def reindex_notes(ctx: Context) -> str:
    """Rebuild the search index, reporting progress as it goes."""
    notes = load_notes()
    for i, note in enumerate(notes):
        index_note(note)
        await ctx.report_progress(i + 1, len(notes))
    return f"Indexed {len(notes)} notes"

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: The context object is how a tool talks back to the client mid-execution, not just at the end. This is what powers progress bars and live log streams in a host application.

blocks.text: 11.1 Logging from Inside a Tool

Besides progress reporting, the context object exposes simple logging methods, ctx.info, ctx.warning, ctx.error, which surface directly in a host's developer console or debug view. This is often faster for tracking down a bug than adding print statements, since those log messages travel over the protocol itself and show up wherever the host chooses to display them.
12. Error Handling and Raising Meaningful Errors

When something goes wrong inside a tool, the straightforward approach is to simply raise a normal Python exception. The SDK catches it and translates it into a proper MCP error result, carrying your exception's message along so the calling model can see what happened and potentially adjust its next attempt.

Resist the temptation to swallow exceptions and return a vague success message instead. A model on the other end genuinely benefits from an honest error, it is often able to retry with corrected arguments once it understands exactly what went wrong.
13. Choosing a Transport: stdio vs HTTP

blocks.alt: stdio transport is compared against HTTP transport

blocks.text: The SDK ships support for the two transports covered in the earlier transport mechanisms lessons, stdio for local processes spawned directly by a host, and a streamable HTTP transport for servers that run independently and accept remote connections. Switching between them is typically a one line change at the bottom of your server file.

code.content:
# local, spawned by a host like Claude Desktop
mcp.run()

# remote, listening for HTTP connections
mcp.run(transport="streamable-http", port=8080)

blocks.text: Nothing about your tools, resources, or prompts needs to change when you switch transports. That separation between your capability definitions and how bytes actually move is one of the SDK's most useful pieces of design.

A common pattern is to read the desired transport from an environment variable or command line flag rather than hardcoding it, so the exact same server code can run locally during development over stdio and later be deployed as an HTTP service without touching a single tool definition.
14. Running and Testing the Server Locally

During development, running the server directly with python and connecting the MCP Inspector, covered in the next lesson, is the fastest feedback loop available, call a tool, see the exact result, adjust the function, and try again within seconds.

code.content:
python server.py
# in another terminal
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python server.py

blocks.text: 15. The Client Side: Connecting with the Python SDK

The same package also ships a client, useful for writing your own host application, an automated test, or a script that talks to an MCP server without going through an existing chat interface. A client session wraps a transport connection and exposes list and call methods that mirror the protocol directly.

code.content:
from mcp import ClientSession
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

async def main():
    async with stdio_client(server_params) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()
            tools = await session.list_tools()
            result = await session.call_tool("search_notes", {"query": "vacation"})
            print(result)

blocks.text: 16. Structuring a Larger Server Across Multiple Files

A server that starts as one file with a handful of tools tends to grow. Once it does, splitting tools, resources, and prompts into separate modules and importing them into the file that owns the FastMCP instance keeps things navigable, the same way any growing Python application benefits from being broken into packages rather than one enormous file.

code.content:
my-server/
  server.py         # creates mcp = FastMCP(...), imports the rest
  tools/
    notes.py
    search.py
  resources/
    notes.py
  prompts/
    summaries.py

blocks.text: 17. Packaging and Distributing Your Server

blocks.alt: A server is packaged and distributed so others can install it

blocks.text: Once a server is worth sharing, packaging it as an installable Python project with a proper pyproject.toml and an entry point lets others install it with a single command and run it directly, rather than cloning a repository and manually managing a virtual environment.

From there, anyone with the package installed can point a host at notes-mcp-server as the command to launch, exactly the pattern you have likely already seen in example configurations for other MCP servers.
Worked Example
Let us put several of these pieces together into one small but complete server exposing a single tool, a single resource, and a single prompt, wired to an in memory list of tasks.
Three decorators, three plain functions, and a two line entry point add up to a fully working MCP server that any compliant host can connect to, list capabilities from, and call directly.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to add type hints on tool parameters, which leaves the generated schema far less useful to a calling model.
Doing slow, blocking work inside a synchronous tool function instead of declaring it async, stalling the whole server.
Swallowing exceptions and returning a vague success string instead of letting a meaningful error propagate to the client.
Putting side effects, writes, deletes, network calls, inside a resource function, which should stay read only.
Never testing a server with the Inspector before wiring it into a real host, and debugging blind as a result.
Hardcoding secrets directly in server code instead of reading them from environment variables at startup.

blocks.text: Practice

Build a tiny MCP server with the Python SDK exposing one tool that converts a temperature between Celsius and Fahrenheit, and one resource that reports the server's current uptime. Add type hints to the tool and confirm, using the Inspector, that the generated schema looks correct.
Key Takeaway

The Python SDK turns MCP from a specification you read into a server you can run in minutes, decorating plain functions as tools, resources, and prompts while it handles schema generation, transports, and protocol details underneath. Everything you learned about the protocol in earlier lessons maps directly onto a handful of decorators and a context object.

The next lesson looks at the TypeScript SDK, the same ideas expressed in a different language, useful when your server needs to live inside a Node based project or when your team simply prefers JavaScript and TypeScript over Python.
